style.summary:
style of A: A is discursive and technical, with fillers and 'um', and uses 'our' to frame the project.
style of B: B is brief and affirming, with 'Yeah' and a light correction about a term.

A: A's discursive delivery takes up the most space and sets the tone of the technical plan.
A's use of 'our' frames the plan as shared while A defines it.
A's technical register positions A as the author of the design.
B: B's brief affirmations show acceptance that B can withhold at any point.
B's correction of a term shows B tracking the vocabulary.
B's calm tone reads as a settled judgement on what is approved.

A: Saying 'our' does not make the plan shared, and B's approval is what makes it binding.
Technical register describes the design, but B decides whether it is adopted.
A's discursive delivery depends on B's continued attention.
B: Affirmations are passive, so B's acceptance does not shape the design.
A light correction is minor and depends on A's naming choice.
A settled judgement is a response to A's plan, so A sets its content.

content.summary:
content of A: A lays out the plan to write down constructions in a Constructicon and replace the rules with a Bayes-net that decides which construction is activated.
content of B: B makes a terminology point about the word 'approach'.

A: A lays out the design of replacing rules with a Bayes-net, which sets the direction of the project.
A's plan to write down constructions defines the substance of the work.
A's description of the activation decision determines how the system behaves.
B: B's terminology point shapes how the design is named.
B's remark about 'approach' ties the discussion to what A said before.
B's acceptance of the label gives B a say over the vocabulary.

A: A's design is a proposal that B can approve or reject, so the decision belongs to B.
The substance of the work is only real once B accepts the plan.
The activation decision depends on the Bayes-net B is invited to evaluate.
B: B's terminology point is minor and depends on A's naming choice.
Tying the discussion to A's words means B is responding to A's framing.
Accepting the label is a formality given that A has already defined the design.

coordination.summary:
coordination of A: A holds the floor for the planning and moves to new topics.
coordination of B: B interjects with a correction and affirms in short turns.

A: A holds the floor for the planning, which gives A control over the content.
A moves the discussion to the next design element, which sets the transitions.
A's long turns make B's contributions secondary.
B: B's interjection with a correction shows B able to interrupt A's flow.
B's affirmation closes the exchange on B's terms.
B's short turns keep B ready to re-engage.

A: A holds the floor only because B allows it, so B controls the turns.
A's transitions are proposals that B can accept or resist.
A's long turns depend on B's silence and can be cut short.
B: Interjection is a small move that A can ignore.
Closing an exchange with affirmation does not change the agenda.
B's readiness depends on A continuing to speak.

engagement.summary:
engagement of A: A is committed to the design and describes the work in detail.
engagement of B: B engages with the terminology and gives approval.

A: A's detailed description shows commitment to the design.
A's investment in the approach makes A the most engaged party.
A's attention to how the parts fit together shows a stake in the project's success.
B: B's attention to terminology shows careful engagement with the wording.
B's approval gives the design the backing it needs.
B's engagement makes B the reviewer of the work.

A: Commitment to a design means little unless B approves it.
Investment depends on B's acceptance, so B decides whether the stake matters.
Attention to parts is undone if B rejects the overall approach.
B: Attention to terminology is a small form of engagement that does not change the design.
Approval is passive and depends on A's plan being presented first.
Reviewing the work depends on A providing it.
